etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English inland, inlond, from Old English inland, equivalent to in- +‎ land. Compare West Frisian ynlân (“inland”), German Inland (“inland”), Danish indland (“inland”), Swedish inland (“inland”), Norwegian innland (“inland”). Compare also Dutch binnenland.

definitions.definition: Within the land; relatively remote from the ocean or from open water; interior.

quote.citation: 1590, Edmund Spenser, “Book II, Canto VI”, in The Faerie Queene. […], London:  […]  [John Wolfe] for William Ponsonbie, →OCLC, stanza 10, page 259:
quote.text: In this wide Inland ſea, that hight by name / The Idle lake, my wandring ſhip I row,  […]

quote.citation: c. 1596–1598 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Merchant of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act V, scene i]:
quote.text: So doth the greater glory dim the less:A substitute shines brightly as a king Unto the king be by, and then his state Empties itself, as doth an inland brook Into the main of waters.

quote.citation: 1785, William Cowper, “Book V. The Winter Morning Walk.”, in The Task, a Poem, […], London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson;  […], →OCLC, page 221:
quote.text: Brutes  […]  / Ruminate heedleſs of the ſcene outſpread / Beneath, beyond, and ſtretching far away / From inland regions to the diſtant main.

quote.citation: 1904–1906, Joseph Conrad, “The Nursery of the Craft”, in The Mirror of the Sea, 1st American edition, New York, N.Y., London: Harper & Brothers, published October 1906, →OCLC, pages 254–255:
quote.text: Happy he who, like Ulysses, has made an adventurous voyage; and there is no such sea for adventurous voyages as the Mediterranean—the inland sea which the ancients looked upon as so vast and so full of wonders.

definitions.definition: Limited to the land, or to inland routes; not passing on, or over, the sea
Confined to one country or state; domestic; not foreign.
(archaic) Of a sophisticated background, especially as relates to a royal court or national capital.

quote.citation: c. 1598–1600 (date written), William Shakespeare, “As You Like It”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene vii]:
quote.text: You touch'd my vein at first: the thorny point of bare distress hath ta'en from me the show of smooth civility; yet am I inland bred, and know some nurture.

quote.citation: c. 1598–1600 (date written), William Shakespeare, “As You Like It”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene ii]:
quote.text: I have been told so of many; but indeed an old religious uncle of mine taught me to speak, who was in his youth an inland man; one that knew courtship too well, for there he fell in love.

definitions.definition: The interior part of a country.

quote.citation: 1599 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Life of Henry the Fift”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene ii]:
quote.text: a wall sufficient to defend Our inland from the pilfering borderers.

definitions.definition: Into, or towards, the interior of the land, away from the coast.

quote.citation: 1836, Sharon Turner, The History of England […] :
quote.text: The greatest waves of population have rolled inland from the east.
